newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major dismisses polls, says Labour "flaky".
newsitem.headline: UK's Major dismisses polls, says Labour "flaky".

text.p: Prime Minister John Major on Friday dismissed his dismal opinion poll showing in Britain's May 1 election campaign and accused the opposition Labour Party's spending plans of being "flaky."
Major said the manifesto unveiled by Labour leader Tony Blair on Thursday had a gap of least 1.5 billion pounds ($2.46 billion) between its tax and spending plans.

"Tony hasn't yet to face any of the difficult decisions. When he is tackled on detail and policy, it seems to me they are rather flaky," said Major, who is bidding to give the Conservatives an unprecedented fifth election victory in a row.

With the Conservatives trailing Labour by up to 24 percentage points in the latest polls, Major is trying desperately to repeat his 1992 success when attacks on Labour's tax policy scared voters away from Labour at the last minute.
"I seem to recall being told last time that I couldn't win and we won comfortably," said Major.
Blair, who has dumped much of Labour's socialist dogma as he battles Major for the middle ground in British politics, pledged his party would not be held to ransom by its trade union paymasters.

Writing in the tabloid Sun newspaper which has switched its allegiance to Labour, Blair said: " I have not created New Labour to see a Labour government give away power to the unions or any other vested interests."
One of the main lines of attack by the Conservatives in the campaign so far has been warning voters that Blair's party will return to its old-style socialist ways if it takes power.

"We will not be held to ransom by the unions," said Blair, pointing out that trade union funding of his party had fallen from 90 percent in 1990 to less than a third last year. On Friday it is the turn of the centrist Liberal Democrats to lay out their political wares before 43.9 million voters.
Unlike their main rivals, they have pledged to raise income tax by one percentage point to finance improvements in education, one of the most sensitive issues in the election.

"Elections are about choices. There is a very clear choice which both Conservatives and Labour are ducking. In the present economic climate you cannot have tax cuts and better public services." their leader Paddy Ashdown told BBC Radio.

"Our choice is to say instead of having temporary tax cuts we should be investing in education, to solve the crisis in our health service," he added. Liberal Democrats are 2,000-1 outsiders to win the election.
Both financial markets and political analysts believe that only a last-minute gaffe can deprive Labour of victory after almost two decades in the political wilderness.
